titleStmt.title: Finding the Right Tools: The Challenges of Digitizing a Twentieth-Century Bengali Periodical

dhq:abstract.p: This article examines the challenges of digitizing Bengali language texts using existing digital tools. By using infrastructure as an analytic frame, the article argues that as the text unsettles and exceeds the capabilities of digital infrastructure, the latter registers them through the discourse of mistakes and errors; what the material conditions making possible the process of digitization cannot read, it renders as broken and illegible. In order to anchor these questions, the article turns to a case study—the process of creating a scholarly digital edition of Betar Jagat (Wireless World), a twentieth-century Bengali periodical—using Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) guidelines and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to translate an image of a page into a searchable text. It demonstrates that both elements of the digital infrastructure, OCR and TEI, rely on the structure of the Latin alphabet in general, and English semantics in particular, thereby affecting not just the processing of print texts and manuscripts to make them machine readable, but also the ways in which the reader’s perception of the page is itself radically altered.

dhq:teaser.p: This article examines the challenges of digitizing texts written in Bengali (which is an abugida script) with existing digital tools, using infrastructure as an analytical frame.

body.p: One of the first issues of Betar Jagat (Wireless World), the mouthpiece for the Calcutta Radio Station, begins with two advertisements encouraging readers of the journal to buy radio valves manufactured by the Marconi company and sold by The Indian Radio and Telegraph Company. The advertisements appear first in English and then in Bengali in the third issue of the journal, published on Friday, 25 October 1929. In itself, these two pages are fairly commonplace—Betar Jagat ran on an average one or two advertisements per page of text, using the revenue generated to sustain publication, and more often than not, these advertised radio-related products. At first glance, the layout of the advertisements is unremarkable as well — no images, just a few words printed on a bare page arranged such that the words appear in the middle of the page (see Figure 1).

figure.head: Advertisement for Marconi’s radio valves published in Betar Jagat, October 25, 1929. The image shows the orthographic variant for the work সর্বত্র (arbatra or everywhere, but in this instance spelled with an additional ব or <word">b.
figure.figDesc: Advertisement for Marconi’s radio valves published in Betar Jagat, October 25, 1929, in abugida script.

body.p: The only point of interest for the contemporary reader appears to be the Bengali version with the spelling of the word সর্বত্র (sarbatra, everywhere). This instance of the word has an unorthodox spelling with the conjunction ব্ব (the two b’s emphasizing the consonant) used instead of the letter ব. That this way of spelling the word cannot be typed using most available technology is at the heart of the argument in this article. Most existing Bengali keyboards cannot accommodate the conjunction ব্ব with the reph or the diagonal slash that appears above ব in the more contemporary instance of the word’s spelling. For this instance, I tried to spell the word using the following keyboards: Avro, MS Word’s Bengali keyboard, and Mac OS’s Bengali keyboard. An online keyboard such as Lexilogos is able to type the word, however, it is not a consistently accurate keyboard, and moreover, the process requires typing the word into Lexilogos’ own textbox, and then copying and pasting it into a word processor such as MS Word, which often leads to a loss of characters owing to the processor’s own formatting idiosyncrasies. The method I used for this paper is to spell the conjoint letters using a word in which the formation is more conventionally found, such as আব্বা (abba, the Urdu word for father), and then copying the conjunction as an isolated unit. Standing in for an <word">r preceding a consonant, the reph, creates a conjunct consonant, and while the addition of another ব does not perceptibly alter how the word sounds when spoken out loud, the combined letter is a significant orthographic element whose absence is striking and warrants discussion because it cannot be represented on screen.

I begin this discussion on encoding Bengali texts with the example of conjunct letters or juktakkhor as these have historically been difficult to render in print, and, later, on digital screens, requiring complex substitutions that often involved altering spellings to suit available technology. As far back as the late 1770s, when Panchanan Karmakar, along with Charles Wilkins, cut some of the earliest wooden Bengali type, we find deliberations over how best to work around conjunct letters given the challenges in reproducing them in print. Karmakar, who designed the first Bengali typeface for Nathaniel Halhed’s A Grammar of the Bengali Language (Halhed 1778), drew on his experience as a blacksmith (karmakar) engraving Bengali calligraphy on metal to create the intricate combinations of letters for the letterpress. In this early iteration, print technology’s discomfort with conjunct letters is clearly visible with additional spaces between combined letters, or shortened marks breaking up the continuity of letters. The challenge, as Fiona Ross suggests, is a fundamental disjuncture arising from a need to find European solutions to the typographic problems posed by Indian writing systems(Ross 1999, p. 39). The discussion over how to represent juktakkhor in print continues well into the twentieth century as leading newspapers including Anandabazar Patrika seek to simplify the language by finding ways around conjuncts. The story of how Bengali linotype developed is the subject of Fiona Ross’ The Printed Bengali Character and Its Evolution where she discusses the socio-cultural impact of typesetting during the print and then digital era (Ross 1999). Ross discusses the particular case of Anandabazar Patrika to highlight the dissonance between tools and the Bengali alphabet. While the history of Bengali typefaces deserves to be a subject of scholarship in its own right, my interest here is in the dissonance between the technology used and the language to which it is applied. From the late seventeenth century onwards, when one finds the earliest examples of Bengali type in texts such as Thomas Goüye’s Observations physique et mathematique (Goüye 1692), to Nathaniel Halhed’s A Code of Gentoo Laws (Halhed 1776), to the mid-twentieth century Monotype printing method, and finally to early computer keyboards, little, if any attention is paid to developing input or output methods dictated by the script and its internal logistics. As one enters the digital era, the incompatibility between script and technology becomes even more apparent with the addition of the computer keyboard, a software capable of making keystrokes machine readable, and fonts which can adequately display letterforms on screen.

I present this preamble as a way to contextualise the discussion that follows, which will suggest that digitizing a Bengali text, despite the considerable progress made in the development of digital technology, is still fraught with the same problems that nineteenth and twentieth-century compositors faced when working with the script; namely, that the tools cannot adequately render the text on either the printed or the digitized page. The digitizing process, instead of making the text available in a different medium, leads to the text becoming invisible, even as one’s attention is drawn more to the tool and the object being digitized. I have in mind here the work of the Critical Infrastructure Studies Collective which invites an engagement with the material conditions making possible our socio-technical systems. From the Critical Infrastructure Studies website which can be found here: https://cistudies.org/about/. As Alan Liu, one of the founding members of the Collective, notes, infrastructure is the social-cum-technological milieu that at once enables the fulfillment of human experience and enforces constraints on that experience, emphasizing the need to examine the conditions under which digital humanities (DH) can, or cannot, be practiced (Liu et al, 2026). Infrastructure as an analytic allows us to understand how cultural objects — both digital and analogue — move through the physical world via material systems that enable their circulation, and how this movement determines the forms assumed by these objects. Marshall McLuhan’s Understanding Media is a seminal text here even though he does not specifically use the term infrastructure (McLuhan 1994). Also of note is Lisa Parks and Nicole Starosielski’s edited volume Signal Traffic collating essays on a variety of infrastructural moments in the geopolitical circulation of electronic media (Parks et al 2015).

Drawing thus on the infrastructural turn in DH and Media Studies, I argue that investigating the gap between technology and texts makes visible the infrastructural substrate of digitization that would otherwise have remined hidden. The work of the Critical Infrastructure Studies Collective intersects productively with Anne McGrail, Angel David Nieves, and Siobhan Senier’s People, Practice, Power: Digital Humanities outside the Center (McGrail et al 2022), while the special issue for Social Text titled Reading for Infrastructure: Worlds Made and Broken edited by Adriana Michele Campos Johnson and Daniel Nemser conceptualizes infrastructure as a textual analytic (Johnson et al 2022). This underlying layer, which includes software, hardware, physical locations of data centres, as well as the networks connecting them, affords a hierarchical conception of digitization; infrastructure resides beneath or behind the referents that it connects within a net or a system. Without this infrastructure, the digital landscape as we experience it would not exist, nor would our conceptions of legible and illegible data, convenient and inconvenient technologies. For those working in Anglophone traditions or Latinate languages, infrastructure is a non-event precisely because it functions as expected, and in doing so remains invisible. The material they work with is recognized and supported by this substrate, and thus the digital infrastructure can hum steadily in the background, never making its presence felt, like a good wi-fi connection, or a keyboard whose characters match the letters on the screen.

It is only when one turns to texts in languages from the Global South that the infrastructure becomes visible as fissures in a system that cannot accommodate these objects. This article suggests that as the text unsettles and exceeds the capabilities of digital infrastructure, the latter registers them through the discourse of mistakes and errors; what the material conditions making possible the process of digitization cannot read, it renders as broken and illegible. This reorients the reading practice whereby one reads for errors rather than content, as non-Latinate fonts such as Bengali appear as impediments to their own digitization. Thus, digital corpora from the Global South are limited because the tools used to create this body of texts rely almost exclusively on Latinate (read, English) languages. When confronted with non-Latinate languages, digital tools approach these texts as problems to be solved using a linguistic system external to them, rather than as a composite body of knowledge in their own right. I suggest that the infrastructural approach allows us to rethink the relationship between digital representation and texts from the Global South as one of hierarchical imbalance and illegibility. Existing digital technology not only prioritizes the Latin alphabet, but more significantly, places the non-Latinate as outside the digital norm. By critically analyzing infrastructure, we can rethink the illegible page not as broken or error-filled, but rather as a product of a set of colonial/postcolonial relations that harken back to the language policies of the British empire.

These claims build on Roopika Risam’s assertion that the digital cultural record is […] complicated by the fact that the politics of digital knowledge production are not neutral but are mired instead in the material and political legacies of colonialism (Risam 2019, p. 23). In this examination of Bengali as challenging the limits of digital infrastructure, I draw on the work of Postcolonial DH scholars like Risam to highlight the Anglophone context within which these tools are developed and applied, and which continues to position Indic languages as peripheral. What is significant for this context is not that Bengali is the seventh most widely spoken language in the world, but that it is visually irregular when compared to the Latin alphabet, and this irregularity inconveniences the infrastructure. The power imbalance caused by the digital world’s Anglocentrism is the subject of a growing body of scholarship which includes an examination of the South Asian technospace (Gajjala and Mitra 2008), of the infrastructure of digital archives (Risam 2019) (Thorat 2019) (Sneha 2022), and of the allure of connectivity and access (Shah 2024) (Bhattacharyya 2022) to name only a few. In positioning this essay alongside this scholarship, I do not wish to argue that the case for Bengali is wholly exceptional. Instead, I place Bengali texts’ entanglements with the digital infrastructure on a continuum with analyses that call for a granular assessment of points of dissonance. Examining specific places where tools used to digitize cultural documents from the Global South fails allows us to understand the systemic underpinnings of such failure.

This article, then, offers a sustained and technically detailed case study that demonstrates where such systemic failure occurs, using two tools in particular — Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI). OCR converts an image of a text, such as a scanned document, into machine-actionable text by identifying marks on the page as letters, numbers or symbols, and then grouping them into words and sentences. TEI, on the other hand, is an internationally accepted standard that uses markup language to define data into a hierarchical structure. While for most Anglophone and Latinate language projects they form merely the first two steps in the workflow that prepare a text for digital manipulation, for under-resources languages from the Global South, they become infrastructural obstacles to be overcome. I anchor this problem in the specific condition of a Bengali language text, Betar Jagat—the publication with which I began this discussion — and examine how its entry into the digital world is limited by the disjuncture between available digitizing tools and the language’s script. The goal of the case study is preservation and access to a cultural record. However, my interest here is the material and intellectual challenges made visible through the digitizing process, as the project workflow becomes oriented to find ways of circumventing the failure of infrastructure to accommodate the text.

The study mentioned above aims to create a digitally manipulable repository of this popular early 20th-century Bengali periodical such that users can query, search, and visualize the pages. This article considers a pilot project of approximately 20 pages taken from two issues of Betar Jagat—October 25, 1929 and October 1, 1940. By tagging individual elements on a page using XML markup language, this project creates an archive flexible enough to sustain future interpretive gestures rather than provide a definitive reading of the text. The tags, although time and labour intensive, provide a documentary foundation such that the reader can move through the text in ways that are prompted not by the structure of a page or book, but rather interpretive questions and editorial decisions embedded in the markup itself. However, as this article demonstrates, both elements of the digital infrastructure, OCR and TEI, rely on the structure of the Latin alphabet in general, and English semantics in particular, thereby affecting not just the processing of print texts and manuscripts to make them machine readable, but also the ways in which the reader’s perception of the page is itself radically altered. I argue here that the dissonance between technology and text positions the latter as flawed and in need of repair, compelling the reader to read pages through the lens of errors and misrecognition.

In what follows, I attend first to OCR and its propensity to either situate Indic language texts as illegible, or to constrain them as images from which individual letters and words cannot be extrapolated. Using examples from the application of a set of open access OCR tools, the discussion highlights the scope of the problem for a project scaled over thousands of pages. Turning then to TEI, the paper demonstrates how language attributes such as XML:lang might begin the process of accommodating linguistic variations in a text, or even non-Latinate languages, but ultimately they are still inadequate for complex texts such as the one under consideration. Here I draw on the paucity of TEI projects in under-resourced languages to demonstrate the tool’s imbricatedness in the Anglophone ecosystem subtending much of DH. I am indebted to the reviewers of this piece for the phrase Anglophone ecosystem which so aptly captures the socio-linguistic environment within which one encodes texts. By way of conclusion, I return to infrastructure as an analytic framework for digital humanities projects from and of the Global South, and what such an orientation might have to offer to the field.

At this point, a brief methodological overview of the case study is in order. For this pilot project, I chose to digitize representative selections from the editorial section and the programme listings from two issues of Betar Jagat. My goal here was to begin comparing the evolution of the magazine using these anchor points, and to examine how Betar Jagat changed to accommodate developments in radio technology and audience tastes. The limited scope of the pilot project was to also provide a sense of the time and labour required for the digitization of a bulk, if not the entirety of the magazine’s available publication run. Approximately 20 pages were digitized, and I included advertisements if they fell within either section. The workflow involved accessing the freely available issues from Google Books, applying i2OCR, India Typing, and Bengali OCR to create and compare the scanned images as machine readable text, manually correcting OCR output, deciding upon the TEI tags to be used in the encoding process, and manually keying in the content into oXygen XML editor 27.1 using the Google Books scanned pages and corrected OCT output as reference points. Language changes were indicated using <xml:lang>, with Bengali used as the default for the project, while programme times mapped onto the <time> tag, and <s> was used for sentences. For advertisements, the <space> tag indicates location of significant images on the page. I chose minimal markup tags within the TEI P5 schema both to maintain consistency across a large volume of transcribed pages, and to allow room for further expansion as the project develops.

div.head: Trying to Read: Optical Character Recognition as Digital Infrastructure
div.p: The uneven distribution of infrastructural resources has been well documented in Digital Humanities. From Alan Liu, Urszula Pawlicka-Deger, and James Smithies’ CFP for an edited volume on Critical Infrastructure Studies and Digital Humanities, The CFP can be found here: https://dhdebates.gc.cuny.edu/page/cfp-critical-infrastructure-studies-digital-humanities#en1 to Anne McGrail, Angel David Nieves, and Siobhan Senier’s People, Practice, Power: Digital Humanities outside the Center, and Domenico Fiormonte, Sukanta Chaudhuri, and Paola Ricaurte’s Global Debates in the Digital Humanities, there is a growing body of scholarship attending to the conscious and unconscious designs determining questions of access and legibility across the North/South axis (Liu et al 2026) (McGrail et al 2022) (Fiormonte et al 2022). One of the areas where this asymmetry frequently manifests itself is in the act of translating print into machine readable digital formats, given its reliance on recognizing individual components of an alphabet. OCR technology has progressed as far as to be able to read Latinate scripts with considerable ease, and is usually the first step in a print-to-digital project requiring little to no manual supervision. Yet for a Bengali language project of the scale and complexity considered in this article, OCR tools are themselves the first of many infrastructural hurdles.

To place the digitization project in context, a few words on Betar Jagat and its cultural significance are in order. First published in September 1929, the magazine was more than a programme journal including editorials, opinion pieces, scripts of popular plays and radio shows, letters from audiences, technological reviews, fiction, and advertisements for everything from radio parts to makeup. While predominantly a Bengali publication, Betar Jagat regularly published English text in the form of articles and advertisements. The bimonthly magazine ran well into the 1980s after which both radio and the publication gave way to television. Thus, even conservatively speaking, Betar Jagat’s archive comprises over 3700 issues cataloguing the aesthetic and political lives of late and postcolonial Bengalis as filtered through radio technology. Short stories and novels serialized in Betar Jagat have been published as edited volumes, with the narrative format offering an organic editorial framework. Some of these are Betar Jagat: Sera Prabandha Sankalan (Betar Jagat: Collection of Best Essays) edited by Amit Chakavorty and Krishnasarbari Dasgupta (Chakavorty and Dasgupta 2000), Betar Jagat: Sera Galpo Sankalan (Betar Jagat: Collection of Best Stories) edited by Amit Chakraborty and Shovan Pathak (Chakraborty and Pathak 2023), and Nirbachita Betar Jagat (Selected Betar Jagat) edited by Ajit Basu (Basu 2015). However, these publications do little more than note date and issue when the issue first appeared in the magazine, eschewing contextual information in favour of narrative continuity.

Yet despite its cultural significance, Betar Jagat is a uniquely challenging document to study. It is simultaneously a text that one can find freely on Google Books, and that is considerably difficult to locate in a physical archive. In a personal conversation with library staff at Akashvani Kolkata (the current iteration of what used to be Calcutta Radio Station), I learnt that physical copies of Betar Jagat occupy a grey area in the library’s holdings. The physical books themselves were originally transported to the Central Archives of Prasar Bharati in New Delhi where they were digitized in their current format, although the exact date for this transformation was not available. As these copies made their way back to Akashvani Kolkata, some were damaged, sometimes beyond repair such that they had to be placed off limits for preservation. To add to this, the original digital files and the physical texts are placed behind layers of red tape, making it nearly impossible for individual readers to access the texts. To give a sense of the layers of bureaucratic control separating the researcher from the archive, I only mention that at the time of writing this article, international scholars have to obtain clearance from the Ministry of External Affairs in New Delhi to even begin the process of applying for access. For Indian academics, this step is not required, but even then, getting a response from Prasar Bharati, the media and information wing of the Indian government, acknowledging receipt of the emailed application is a herculean task in and of itself. While extensive, the Google Books collection does have gaps, some of which can be filled using extant copies digitized on Internet Archive as part of the Public Library of India collection. Physical copies are sometimes held in personal collections, although most of these date from the 1960s and 70s, and are sporadic in the issues and volumes they contain. However, by juxtaposing these digital and physical collections, one can begin to recreate a fairly extensive archive of the journal’s issues.

These collections thus offer an invaluable, if somewhat limited resource since there is little archival information provided on either site, and the personal collections are not archived either. Neither do the digitized pages follow any clear organizational logic. On Google Books, the only metadata provided indicates the date of publication and lists Akashvani or All India Radio as the publisher, but gives no account of the provenance of the pages or an explanation as to missing issues. Some issues appear in bound volumes with the binding obstructing text on the inner edges, while others bear page marks such as library stamps distorting texts and images. Internet Archive’s collection does identify when the texts were digitized (2022), and provides an overview of the languages present in print, but it is unclear if the digitizing process for both sites was the same one as mentioned by the Akashvani Kolkata library staff.

What one has here, then, is a starting point whereby readers can access parts of the Betar Jagat collection digitally, but their interaction with the publication is limited by the few options provided by either Google Books or Internet Archive. For example, while one can search for specific words within a particular issue using Google Books Reader’s search function, the OCR tool used by the site is liable to miss occurrences of the word when the print is not entirely clear, when there is a variation in spelling, or when there are too many elements on a page. Similarly, the annotating tool is irregular in its ability to identify words and phrases, frequently including blank space in place of text. Following its conventions of accessible information, Internet Archive uses hOCR, which is an open-source OCR program using markup language to store textual data, but most of the generated files render meaningless texts. Thus, while the digital copies on Google Books and Internet Archive provide at least an initial look at the publication, any serious scholarship still requires a more sustained and cohesive digitizing process, allowing one to search, compare, and otherwise manipulate the digital files.

In order to create a digital scholarly edition of Betar Jagat, one needs to identify a set of tools that can extract plain text from images, express this text in some form of a searchable, organized schema, and finally display the text such a user can search for patterns in the text. Even though Google Books’ proprietary OCR Vision API is far from reliable, it offers a plausible starting point in our search for more developed OCRs capable of handling poorly visible, multi-column data. Google Books’ in-built OCR system, or their proprietary Cloud Vision API, presents another logistical hurdle in that the text read by these OCRs cannot then be copied onto another platform such as an XML editor, making the OCR transcribed text virtually useless. Thus while the success rate in character recognition is much higher with these proprietary OCRs, in practice I discount them precisely because the source code is owned and controlled by a company, and the generated data is not transferable across platforms. While OCR technology has developed rapidly in the last few years with numerous free and paid varieties, the vast majority of these applications have limited success with Indic texts. Scholars gave long noted the absence of viable options leading to substantial research in the field, but most, if not all OCR tools, either designed for Bengali in particular, Enhancement of Bengali OCR by Specialized Models and Advanced Techniques for Diverse Document Types, by AKM Shahariar Azad Rabby, among others, details the process of designing a bespoke OCR for Bengali which can both attend to the alphabet’s internal logic, while also preserving the layout of the page (Rabby 2024). or repurposed from other applications Zahra Rizvi, Rohan Chauhan, A. Sean Pue, and Nishat Zaidi’s Minimal Computing for Exploring Indian Poetics, offers a few suggestions including eScriptorium, an experimental OCR/HTR (Handwritten Text Recognition) model developed by the eScripta team (Chauhan et al 2022). exist as prototypes and are thus outside the reach of most projects not directly working with a software development team. Existing OCRs such as i2OCR, India Typing, or Bengali OCR are apt to produce illegible results, with conjuncts being the primary hurdle which these applications are unable to read. Consider, for example, the following set of scanned text as rendered by Bengali OCR, a freely available tool (see Figure 2 and Figure 3).

div.p: As the images show, the OCR rendition distorts conjunct words such as অস্ট্রেলিয়া (Australia) turning it into a nonsense word অস্টেলিয়া (Austelia) by missing the র ফলা or the r consonant conjunct creating the sound tra. It even misreads the word সমস্ত (all or whole) as সমন্ত mistaking the conjunct স্ত (st) for the visually similar ন্ত (nt), leading to yet another meaningless word. These details come after the OCR misreads the very date of the issue’s publication owing to a design choice in the original. On an average, all three OCRs misread words once or twice every three lines of text, with a higher failure rate when it comes to combined letters and vowel marks. For this pilot project, the three OCRs were tested on each digitized page, totalling a number of 20 pages, and the failure rate was more or less consistent across the pages. Thus for a section of 40 words, the OCRs misread about 4-5 words, with a Word Error Rate of approximately 10%. While this may not strike one as a particularly high failure rate when looking at one or two issues, if one scales the project overs thousands of pages, the scope of the problem becomes a practical hinderance. These numbers are consistent with other attempts at using OCR to read Indic language texts, both in print and manuscript version. Saniya Irfan, in her article Developing a TEI-Encoded Digital Archive of 19th-Century Urdu Marsiya: Production and Challenges notes that there is a 10% Word Error Rate when extracting text from Urdu manuscripts using open source OCRs, which must then be added to the time required to review OCRs and manually key in words. The resource can be found here https://zenodo.org/records/13997483 To add to this, one must also consider the minute nature of the misreadings performed by the OCRs, as in the case of বিঘোষিত being read as বিঘোসিত, with ষ being replaced with স. The change is hard to spot initially, but leads to the transcribed word becoming meaningless.

While these are egregious mistakes, other OCRs produce equally garbled text, with one of the fundamental problems being the tool’s inability to read how Bengali is laid out on the page. In her discussion on the shortcomings of existing OCR tools, Purbasha Auddy provides a succinct description of the visual placement of Bengali characters in relation to the page (Auddy 2022). Using her own name as an example, Auddy explains:

Bengali is an abugida script, where vowels take on a modified shape if tagged to a consonant: for instance, প (p, a consonant) + ঊ (u, a vowel) = পূ (pu), the first component of my name in Bengali, পূর্বাশা (Purbasha). The basic consonants প, ব, and শ occupy the middle zone. The vowel tag ূ, representing ঊ (u), is placed below প, extending it to the lower zone. Again, what in full is the letter র I becomes a slanting line above the next consonant (here ব, b) if there is no vowel in between; this conjunct consonant র্ব occupies both the middle and the upper zones. Thus, an OCR tool in Bengali has to recognize many more glyphs than with the Latin or roman alphabet.” (Auddy 2022)

Each glyph that the OCR tool must recognize becomes a possible obstruction, and when one is examining a nineteenth or early twentieth-century text, these hurdles increase manifold owing to the font used in printing. While Betar Jagat uses a relatively modern font as compared to the nineteenth-century periodicals such as Sambad samacār, OCR tools still struggle at character recognition, leaving the scholar with no other option than manually entering the text into plain text format — in essence serving as the human version of an OCR — or extensively cleaning up the results produced by an OCR.

Both options are labour intensive, and they affect what I claim is a reorientation of the reading practice whereby the reader reads for potential obstacles or mistakes. What occurs is not just an epistemically produced invisibility as Sayan Bhattacharyya suggests owing to the tools’ inability to operate within a non-Western knowledge system, but the text becoming visible only through orthographic discrepancies (Bhattacharyya 2022). Instead of reading for meaning, the body of the text now presents itself to the reader as a series of letters and conjuncts, each of which can throw the digitizing process into disarray. Adding to this general sense of reading for mistakes is the need to locate the source of that error — is it created by the OCR tool, or is it, as this article’s opening example suggests, a variation present in the original text itself? In the midst of this process, the issue of Betar Jagat under consideration runs the risk of becoming illegible within a digital schema that compels it to conform to an alphabet system that has no upper or lower zone, and limited experience with an abugida script.

The tool seeks to standardize data according to a knowledge apparatus that prioritizes the Latin alphabet. Anything that does not fit between the lines normally occupied by letters of this alphabet registers as erroneous and in need of restoration or correction. Critical analysis of such a page, then, is mediated by digital infrastructure engineered to represent cultural records from the Global South as deviations from the norm, encouraging the reader’s eye to look for mistakes and misprints instead of aesthetic and technical choices made by producers of the text. The separation between the languages of the Global South and digital infrastructural availability has been the subject of much discussion in Digital Humanities, with scholars largely in agreement about the homogenizing effect of digital tools and practices (Gil and Ortega 2016) (Risam 2019) (Fiormonte 2014) (Dombrowski 2022) (Brown 2023). I draw on this conversation to argue that what is left behind as a result of these interventions is a framework in which texts such as Betar Jagat appear as deviations from the Anglophone norm and are thus peripheral to digital infrastructure. Therefore, before one can process the text for meaningful data, it must be cleaned up and rid of factual inaccuracies, even when these errors have been introduced as a result of the technological interventions. The few projects that take on the task of digitizing textual records from the digital periphery must simultaneously reject the epistemic framing of these texts as congenitally error-filled, while adapting existing approaches to achieve their goals. What they produce is new knowledge while also attempting to have it be recognized as knowledge.

div.head: Arranging the Text: TEI as Digital Infrastructure
div.p: While existing OCRs are an example of infrastructure breaking down and revealing its Anglophone biases, a more promising tool in our attempt at creating a digital scholarly edition of Betar Jagat comes in the guise of the Text Encoding Initiative or TEI guidelines. TEI is a collectively defined set of XML tags designed predominantly by humanities scholars looking for a common standard for encoding electronic texts. TEI P3 was first released in 1994, and since then the guidelines have been regularly updated to accommodate a variety of textual situations. Its current iteration, TEI P5, released in 2011 is the version I use in this case study. It is one of the few tools well-positioned for use in the digitization of texts in non-Latinate languages because as a set of coding guidelines, it recognizes that texts exist in a variety of structural and linguistic formats, and is catholic in its consideration of a text’s age or a font’s provenance. At its core, TEI is an encoding method that uses Extensible Markup Language (XML) to isolate elements on a page using tags or markup as it divides the text into hierarchically linked sections. It offers a standard schema which can be modified to achieve the level of granular transcription required for the project in question, allowing the encoder to identify minute details such as multiple spellings of a word, or to provide a broader overview of the page through larger textual elements such as sentences, paragraphs, and page breaks. Since TEI depends on the encoder to indicate textual elements such as letters and words, the approach can be used on multilingual corpora, with the XML:lang attribute indicating the language of the element being coded. In the case of XML, a tag refers to the markup used to denote elements, with an element being the aspect of the text that is being described. Additional information about elements is inserted through attributes. I draw on TEI: Electronic Text Encoding and Interchange , along with Lou Barnard’s What is the Text Encoding Initiative? for definitions and explanations of technical details.

For a document such as Betar Jagat with 24 issues published annually over the course of more than 50 years, with each issue containing a bewildering array of information, both written and visual, TEI is a particularly suitable tool since by nature both the object being digitized and the implement used rely on a hierarchical organizational structure. Thus, both tools invite users to think of a large body of textual material in terms of how their constituent parts relate to each other — words belonging to sentences or lines, which come together to form paragraphs making up a page in an article or a division in an issue culminating in a volume. Similarly, the page can be imagined in terms of columns of words and images, with each image lending itself to being further subdivided into words and pictures. One could, for example, examine how the morning programmes evolved over the course of the first few years of Betar Jagat, by tagging programme lists using element tags for time of broadcast, name of programme, and list of performers. Once the coded pages are collated and displayed using a suitable platform, the user could notice how not only did broadcast times get earlier and earlier in the day, but that programme variety increased, offering listeners a mix of news and music broadcasts, with talk shows being reserved for later in the day. At the same time, one could potentially also identify patterns in advertisement placement around programme lists, offering another avenue through which an image of the early twentieth-century Bengali radio listener emerges.

div.p: The reason why TEI could be successful at preparing a Bengali text for computational analysis is twofold. On the one hand, it digitizes descriptive markup, a process which has historically always been a part of the printed page in defining a page qua page. As the name suggests, these tags describe or label parts of a document, usually in relation to each other, while procedural markup provides information about formatting. The distinction, originally articulated by Charles Goldfarb in his A Generalized Approach to Document Markup, suggests that descriptive markups are more conceptual in nature, perceiving the text as an author or an editor would, while prescriptive markup falls more in the domain of the typesetter or the publisher (Goldfarb 1981). While the two can, and often, do overlap, viewing TEI as descriptive bolsters the claim that most Digital Humanists make about the method’s editorial bent. On the other hand, the TEI guidelines are not designed to merely produce a faithful record of the text as legible data — which is more the domain of OCR — but rather to create an impression of the page as it is presented to the printer or the reader, inviting the encoder to highlight sections of the page so as to preempt scholarly analysis. As an encoding method, it is necessarily interpretive as it calls for the encoder to determine what counts as parts of the text, what elements require additional editorial comments, and how the text’s structure should be represented. For a detailed introduction to TEI see A Gentle Introduction to TEI. Allen H. Renear’s Text Encoding provides a good overview of the history of descriptive markup (Renear, 2007). For a document such as a popular magazine, this offers the encoder the opportunity to make visible their editorial intervention while simultaneously drawing attention to the myriad forms of texts and images that exist as paratext to the central body of the text. The act of annotating a document thus requires one to simultaneously close and distant read pages, identifying broader textual patterns while filling in those patterns with material at the level of individual words and punctuations.

Yet despite its promise, the Anglophone ecosystem through which TEI guidelines are learnt and disseminated presents an inherent infrastructural flaw. Raffaele Viglianti, Nidia Hernández, Gimena del Rio Riande and Romina De Léon note that digital scholarly editions in the Global South suffer from training material being available almost exclusively in English (Viglianti et al, 2022). I extend this argument to existing support for TEI guidelines — a signal element in numerous Anglophone digital scholarly editions — as well. As of the writing of this article, the TEI website lists 206 projects that use TEI with fewer than 10 of those projects being in non-Latinate languages, approximately 15 projects using material from the Global South, and of those 15, only 1, the African Languages Lexicon Project (ALLEX), in under-resourced languages from the Global South. While this is far from an exhaustive list of projects using TEI, it gives us a representative overview of the predominance of Anglophone and Latinate languages in the field of TEI. While the XML codes themselves can accommodate text regardless of language, in order to learn the process of encoding, one needs to be able to read and work in English to a high degree of fluency. For example, in order to successfully employ the <xml:lang> attribute, the encoder has to parse both the explanations and examples offered on the TEI website, all of which is in English. This requires a semantic and syntactic familiarity with English so as to understand how the attribute has to be nested within the correct element tag each time the language setting needs to be indicated. Yet neither XML coding, nor the TEI guidelines have any necessary technical affiliation with English. Gretchen McCulloch argues that one can make a programming language out of any symbols — the machine is no more Anglophone than one designs it to be — and markup guidelines created by the TEI are premised merely on the nature of a text being an object with hierarchically connected parts (McCulloch 2019). Thus, the disproportionate structural power wielded by Anglophone epistemes means that regardless of how well one knows Bengali, one has to be eminently comfortable in the English language in order to digitize a page in Bengali.

Such dependence on English, then, creates a systemic gap in the number of TEI projects emerging from the Global South. As of the time of writing this article, the TEI website lists 206 projects that use TEI with fewer than twenty of them in non-Latinate languages, approximately fifteen projects using material from the Global South, and of those fifteen, only four, the African Languages Lexicon Project (ALLEX), two Sanskrit and one Tamil projects, in under-resourced languages from the Global South. The two Sanskrit DH projects that use TEI extensively, Search and Retrieval of Indic Texts (SARIT) Led by Dominik Wujastyk, Birgit Kellner, Sheldon Pollock, SARIT examines predominantly, but not exclusively, Sanskrit manuscripts. https://tei-c.org/activities/projects/sarit/ and Digital IndologyAndrew Ollett’s project examines Kannada, Prakrit, and Sanskrit texts at http://prakrit.info/dh/index.html are both housed at the University of Chicago, while Texts Surrounding Texts: Satellite Stanzas, Prefaces and Colophons in South- Indian Manuscripts looks predominantly at Tamil manuscripts, and is a Franco-German effort (Francis and Wilden 2025). The only published Bengali language TEI project is Famine and Dearth in India and Britain, 1550-1800, a joint undertaking by Ayesha Mukherjee from the University of Exeter and Amlan Dasgupta from the School of Cultural Texts and Records (SCTR) at Jadavpur University, with the latter being a pioneering institution in the history of DH in India, and being closely affiliated with the university’s Department of English (Mukherjee and Gupta n.d.). An overview and description for this project can be found here: https://famineanddearth.exeter.ac.uk/index.html While there is a growing body of scholarship arguing for the need to use TEI guidelines to create interactive digital scholarly editions in Hindi, Urdu, and Punjabi, much of this work is still at a nascent stage (Irfan 2026). Saniya Irfan’s Introducing the TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) Framework for Minimal Digital Scholarly Editions presents a compelling case for digitizing Urdu poetry, and Irfan is also a part of the Jugaad CoLab collective that is working towards encoding Hindi and Urdu texts. Compare this to the plethora of TEI projects in English and Latinate languages, ranging from some of the earliest implementations of the guidelines in projects hosted by multiple major institutions from the Global North, The Charles Harpur Critical Archive began life in 2008-09 in collaboration with the University of New South Wales and SCTR, and it was also where I first worked on encoding manuscripts as a Project Fellow at SCTR. The final volume of encoded poems was published in August 2026. More on the project can be found at https://charles-harpur.org/Home/Site/ to simplified versions of TEI aimed at teaching the guidelines to students TEI by Example is a UK based project that offers both simplified tutorials as well as an open source coding platform. The project can be found at https://teibyexample.org/exist/ , and landmark projects that have been field defining Of the many, two of note are The Walt Whitman Archive (https://whitmanarchive.org/) and The Bodleian First Folio (https://firstfolio.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/).—and the scarcity of DH projects from outside the Global North becomes even more noticeable. Combing through the numerous lists posted on university websites, DH conferences and hubs, and classroom projects, one cannot help but note the depth and variety of applications that bring in scholars, students, and citizen scholars.

That the discrepancy is owing to the repercussions of the dissonance between text and tool becomes evident when one considers the second of two documented Bengali language TEI projects. It is an unpublished effort, also housed at SCTR and directed by Amlan Dasgupta, exploring three versions of a single text: Sukumar Ray’s nonsense-satire, Chalachittachanchari; its English translation by Amlan Dasgupta titled The Busy Bee; and the untitled partial Hindi translation by Lav KanoiThese sources were mentioned to me by Bhowmik during an interview with her (Bhowmik 2025). Because the project was not completed, the TEI document and the files are not published at the time of this writing.. Given that Bengali texts are those most frequently digitized when compared to other Indic languages (in no small part owing to the pioneering efforts of SCTR), and that TEI is an accepted and low-tech editorial tool, this paucity signals an infrastructural imbalance. Spandana Bhowmik, one of the collaborators in the Chalachittachanchari project noted in a personal interview that the first hurdle is TEI itself as a tool/method where you need to tag everything extensively to make it work for any purpose […] for the tags, especially the parameters within the tags – if they are in Bengali, they may create problems for the representation/output (Bhowmik 2025). My interview with Bhowmik was conducted via email between May to June 2025; responses were collected in Google Doc format. She stressed that even with bespoke software designed to visual textual variations in documents using both Bengali and English fonts, switching between English and Bengali, either in the form of the XML tags themselves or the marked up content, led to practical problems in creating a digital imprint of the text. Bhowmik refers to Prabhed, the software custom built by SCTR in collaboration with the Department of Computer Science at Jadavpur University in 2009 – 2010, and used most notably in the Bichitra project which collated the print and manuscript works by Rabindranath Tagore. When coupled with the need to manually type in the Bengali text within the tags because OCRs are unreliable, TEI becomes far too labour intensive to be a sustainable method for most projects unsupported by a large institutional infrastructure.

The need to manually [type] the text while tagging differences not only takes a lot of effort and time, as Bhowmik emphasizes, but it reiterates the problem of reading the page as incompatible with existing technology, and renders the Bengali font as digitally elusive (Bhowmik 2025). A signal part of the challenge for the case study considered in this article stems from this combination of the code being written in English and the lack of a reliable plain text version of a page of Betar Jagat. Whether one chooses to clean up a plain text page created using OCR, or to manually type in the words, one has to wrangle with a less than perfect keyboard systems, frequently struggling with not just conjunct letters but also conjoined words. While the TEI Consortium, an international network of scholars and practitioners responsible for developing and maintaining the guidelines, are engaged in translating the instructions and discussions, the XML source code or the syntax rules exists only in English. XML editors, such as Oxygen and Visual Studio Code therefore require the encoder to continually switch between keyboards whether they are copying text into the editor or directly keying it in.

Given that transferring the text also involves making editorial decisions regarding which tags or elements to use, depending on the nature and section of text being coded, one is essentially asking the entire digital system, including the encoder, to be working in at least two languages at all times. When the project is scaled over hundreds, if not thousands of pages, the problem becomes even more acute, and once again we are faced with the reality of errors being introduced into the text through the process of digitization. While a certain degree of human and computer error is always allowed in any large-scale digitizing endeavour, the possibility of creating a misrepresentation of the original page is largely a result of working with non-Anglophone texts. To return briefly to the example with which I open this piece, and to the two different spellings of the word সর্বত্র. Since সর্বত্র is how we spell the word now, each instance of সর্ব্বত্র must now be editorialized upon to indicate that it is not a result of human error, but rather an accurate representation of the page. The variant thus draws attention to itself by being different from accepted usage, suggesting underlying motivation wherever we find it in the text. That both spellings did exist simultaneously, and what is far more fascinating about the instance where the latter occurs has very little to do with the word itself, is a narrative that is now buried under editorial asides and additional XML tags indicating its input history.

I risk belabouring this point about a reorientation of the reader’s relationship to the page to highlight the subtle yet significant changes that are brought to bear upon how one reads the text because of this mismatch between the epistemes to which the tool and the text belong. By compelling the reader to notice and reflect upon a word as an orthographic variation incapable of being recognized by the keyboard, the digital tool changes how the reader looks at the page. Instead of seeing that page as text and images that need to be coded, the reader now perceives the page as a potential minefield, not knowing which variation in spelling will cause the encoding process to be halted for a prolonged period while she hunts for the appropriate solution. In essence, then, the act of reading becomes one of problem spotting and solving, instead of merely the repetitive task of keying in large swaths of textual material.

The need to find solutions at the level of individual words reminds us of Ross’s provocation that the technological challenge here is systemic (Ross 1999). The Bengali language and its orthographic rules are reduced to problems which cannot be successfully processed into knowledge until it has been adequately translated and glossed. While in itself, the act of encoding involves a degree of editorial intervention, and one might argue that the code itself serves as a glossary to a text that has been transmediated into a digital format, my argument here refers to a text’s legibility; the moment we are called on to read the words on a page as incommensurable with the lens applied to the page, at that instance, the language to which those words belong is placed outside comprehension. One is reminded of the debate in Postcolonial Studies of the late 90s – early 2000s of whether or not to gloss words in languages from the Global South, except in this instance the question becomes even more critical — can one even represent these words on the digital page?

div.head: What Infrastructure Reveals
div.p: What this initial foray into Bengali’s entanglement with OCR and TEI reveals are fissures in the digital infrastructure which follows the well-worn path of material infrastructure as a concept rooted in Enlightenment modernity, While scholarship supporting this claim is too prolific to need exhaustive documentation, texts of note include Brian Larkin’s Signal and Noise (Larkin 2008), Roopika Risam’s New Digital Worlds (Risam 2019), and Dhanashree Thorat’s Colonial Topographies of Internet Infrastructure (Thorat 2019). and of the Global North’s hegemonic control over means of production and distribution. We are also provided with a glimpse into the infrastructural dependencies: the need for sheer human labour in a process that is aimed at mechanizing access, version control and proprietary software, and funding exigencies. However bleak the current terrain of digital infrastructure may seem from the above case study, it is far from immutable. Instead, I wish to argue that by critically engaging with the gaps where technology fails its target objects, we are afforded new and creative ways to conceptualize relationality, and to rethink how we would like these objects to move through the world.

If we take this as our starting point, then we can begin the process of developing an architecture for a project based on the needs of the material being digitized and the scholar(s) designing the research questions driving it. These needs are not merely practical, although in appearance they might overwhelmingly be so; rather they are the requirements of scholarship that makes visible its own socio-material contexts as a critical axis of research. This approach begins by asking us to think consciously about the tools we use — how do we come to take these tools for granted, and in doing so, what assumptions are we making about the nature of our scholarly methods? A case in point is using proprietary technologies such as Microsoft Word on Apple computers, and the subsequent circumlocutions one has to make in order to transcribe a page in Bengali. While frustrating at an individual level, the problem demonstrates how scholarship is mediated by available infrastructure, having far reaching consequences on how we see the page and consider what can be represented there. Beyond this, it raises a question about whether we use tools because the projects need them, or because we have become used to working with a particular set of instruments, within an infrastructural paradigm familiar to us, and if the latter, how might we reorient our workflow so as to prioritize that which is necessary to productively explore the research question? If the digital infrastructure cannot sustain the questions we are asking, then regardless of how user friendly they might appear to be, they must be either jettisoned or repurposed to better serve the critical endevaour.

Given the range of material under consideration in the Betar Jagat digitization project, it is important to look at other efforts currently underway so to both study the ways in which they organize their workflows around infrastructural impediments, and to learn from the tools they employ. A concern with constraints, and the practical need to find workarounds informs the Jugaad CoLab project which I discuss earlier in this article, and for these reasons, it presents itself as a viable model (Chauhan et al. 2022). While the project combines an impressive array of reworked tools from different contexts to create machine-readable, genre-specific corpora of Hindi and Urdu texts, its strongest feature is its reliance on citizen scholarship (Rizvi et al. 2022). As digital repositories such as Rekhta and Project Madurai have shown, creation and maintenance of digital archives can be performed by citizen scholars working outside academic affiliations. The Partition Testimonies held at Lahore University of Management Sciences’ Digital Archive, for example, contains interview transcriptions created by academic and non-academic researchers, allowing for a greater distribution of both labour and investment. For the Betar Jagat project, such citizen scholars should be considered as a valuable resource, both at the initial stage of correcting and overseeing OCR output, and at the testing stage for the final collated product. At a practical level, such an approach acknowledges the lack of intensive institutional support, and draws on the publication’s popularity over the course of its sixty years of existence.

For a digitizing project to resonate with readers and users beyond the academy, it needs to retain texts as part of public scholarship. If including citizen scholars is one possible avenue for doing so, then the other is to use and rework open source platforms and software such that both the process and the final output are available to researchers and interested users alike. An open repository such as Zenodo can be used to house, share, and publish the raw dataset and XML codes. While computationally technical, tasks such training an OCR to read the Bengali typescript more consistently (Chauhan 2023) or automating the TEI builder such that the manual tagging process is considerably reduced (Scheithauer et al. 2024) can be learnt through open access tutorials online, expediting the digitizing project. As projects such as the Open Islamicate Texts Initiative (OpenItI) have recently demonstrated, eScriptorium is an open source platform that provides a holistic workflow for digital scholarly editions, and can successfully transcribe handwritten and typed pages in non-Latinate scripts, indicating line and space locations for text. Taken together, such efforts offer specific and concrete models for creating a digital scholarly edition of Betar Jagat.

The adoption of these tools, work processes, and the projects in progress demonstrate the extent to which DH scholars in the Global South in general, and South Asia in particular, have successfully iterated a pluralistic digital humanities that is deeply invested in cross-disciplinary exchanges and pedagogical innovation (Roy and Menon 2022). Such a move offers us a way to reorient ourselves in relation to the infrastructural problems that this article has been grappling with, and perceive these obstacles as real but not insurmountable. As one looks at projects founded in the concept of jugaad born of minimal computing, Minimal computing refers to a set of practices and methods of computing developed to account for infrastructural constraints, such as limited bandwidth, paucity of hardware and software and associated training material, or other factors (Chauhan et al. 2023) (Risam and Gil 2022). to those invested in reimagining the digital archive, While there are too many of these projects to list, some of the notable ones include SCTR’s Bichitra project (https://bichitra.jdvu.ac.in/index.php), the Indian Memory Project (https://www.indianmemoryproject.com/), and the Kerala State Central Library Rare Books Online (http://103.251.43.202/rarebooks/index.php). to exploring open source software capable of working with the nuances of multilayered alphabet systems, The online magazine Digital Orientalist is a comprehensive resource for such projects as indexed by posts on HTR (Chauhan et al 2022) (Griffiths 2025), text processing (Plau 2020) (Butler 2026), and digital mapping (Hayes 2022) (Casalini 2023), to name only a few areas covered by the publication. the work of restructuring available resources becomes more than evident. As these and other projects demonstrate, DH in the Global South has turned emphatically to using open source software where possible, reworking and combining tools, and in essence prioritizing practicality and sustainability as their guiding principles. This in turn has led to greater visibility for the relationship between the cultural record being digitized and digital technology, inviting scholars and practitioners alike to think beyond the Global North’s understanding of the digital infrastructure.
